beginner: Persimmon is easygoing about soil but wants one thing above all: good drainage. A deep, well-drained loam is ideal, and a sandy loam or lighter sandy soil works fine too. The trouble spot is heavy clay that holds water, because persimmon roots, especially on Asian types, are prone to root rot in soggy ground. If your soil is heavy or wet, plant on a raised mound so the roots sit above standing water. A soil of ordinary richness suits it; persimmon needs little feeding and too much can cause the fruit to drop.
seasoned: Persimmon is broadly soil-tolerant but demands good drainage, ideally a deep, well-drained loam; a sandy loam is well suited and lighter sandy soils are workable. Heavy, water-holding clay is the problem texture, since persimmon (especially Diospyros kaki) is susceptible to root and crown rot on poorly drained sites; on such ground plant on a raised berm. Best sites are upland sandy loams. Moderate fertility is plenty, and persimmon is sensitive to salinity and to excess nitrogen, which triggers fruit drop.

beginner: Persimmon does best in a slightly acidic soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5, and is fine up to about 7.0 (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Test your soil before planting the permanent tree. If it is too acidic, garden lime raises the pH; if it is too alkaline, elemental sulfur lowers it. Mix any amendment in before planting, since pH changes slowly and is far easier to correct before the tree is in the ground.
seasoned: Persimmon prefers a slightly acidic pH 6.0 to 6.5 and tolerates up to about 7.0. Test before planting and adjust gradually: lime raises a too-acidic pH, elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Work amendments in ahead of planting the permanent tree, since pH shifts slowly and is easiest to correct before establishment.

beginner: Persimmon barely needs feeding, and too much fertilizer, especially nitrogen, makes the fruit drop off. Go light. Scatter it evenly on the soil around the tree out to where the branches reach, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. On good soil an older tree may need nothing at all, so only feed if the tree looks weak or the leaves are pale.
seasoned: Persimmon needs little feeding and is easily over-fed: excess nitrogen causes premature fruit drop. A light program suits it, split across the season on sandy soils (the bulk in late dormancy, a lighter touch in early and late summer), broadcast evenly around the root zone to the drip line and kept off the trunk. On decent soil an established tree may need no fertilizer at all; feed only if growth is weak or leaves are pale.

beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) is all persimmon needs, and often it needs none. Do not overdo it, because too much, especially the first number, nitrogen, makes the fruit fall off.
seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 is plenty for persimmon; the tree is a light feeder and over-fertilizing, particularly with nitrogen, drops fruit rather than improving it. Err toward less.

beginner: A simple rule is about 2 ounces of 10-10-10 for each year of the tree's age, given in late winter, with a little more in early and late summer if your soil is sandy. Do not feed a tree that is already growing well, and never put fertilizer in the planting hole. If in doubt, feed less: too much makes persimmons drop.
seasoned: A common home rate is about 2 ounces of 10-10-10 per year of tree age, applied in late dormancy (roughly March), with lighter follow-up feedings in early and late summer where the soil is sandy. Cap it at a modest total for a mature tree and do not fertilize at planting. If growth is already vigorous, skip feeding entirely; excess nitrogen shows up as dropped fruit, not bigger crops.

beginner: Most Asian persimmons are self-fruitful, so one tree fruits on its own and you do not need a partner tree. American persimmons are different: they usually have male and female trees, so a female needs a male American persimmon nearby to fruit, unless you plant a self-fruitful kind like Meader. For a tree, the pairings that matter are not vegetable-garden companions but what grows around the roots: keep grass and weeds pulled back from under the branches, since lawn competes with a young tree, and a mulched, weed-free circle helps it settle in. Persimmon is a low-pest, easygoing tree, so there is little else to fuss over.
seasoned: Asian persimmon (D. kaki) is self-fruitful, so a single tree crops without a pollinizer; American persimmon (D. virginiana) is typically dioecious and a female needs a male within roughly 50 to 200 feet, the exception being self-fruitful selections like Meader. The interactions that matter for a tree concern the root zone, not classic vegetable companions: keep turf and weeds cleared back from under the canopy, since grass competes hard with a young tree, and a mulched, competition-free root area speeds establishment. Persimmon is notably low-pest and low-maintenance, so companion planting is a minor consideration here.

beginner: Little bumps stuck to the bark, twigs, and leaf undersides that do not move. White peach scale looks like snow-white crust on the trunk and branches; other scales are small brown domes. They leave a sticky coating (honeydew) that turns black with sooty mold and attracts ants. Bad cases slowly weaken the tree.
seasoned: Small, immobile bumps on bark, twigs, and the underside of leaves; white peach scale shows as snow-white encrustations on the trunk and limbs, while soft scales are brown and rounded. Heavy infestations produce sticky honeydew that blackens with sooty mold and draws ants. Vigor and fruit quality decline where scale builds up unchecked.

beginner: Tiny sap-sucking insects that hide under a waxy shell, mainly white peach scale and soft scales. They feed on the tree's sap and drip sticky honeydew that grows black mold. They get worse when sprays kill off the helpful insects that normally eat them.
seasoned: Several scale species, notably white peach scale and soft scales (Parthenolecanium spp.), which insert their mouthparts and feed on sap under a protective waxy shell. Their honeydew supports sooty mold. Populations flare where natural enemies have been knocked back by broad-spectrum sprays.

beginner: Let the helpful bugs do the work by avoiding broad sprays, since ladybugs and tiny wasps usually keep scale in check on persimmon. Cut out and throw away badly crusted branches. A spray of horticultural oil while the tree is leafless in winter smothers the scale on the bark and is the simplest hands-on control.
seasoned: Preserve natural enemies (ladybugs, parasitic wasps) by not spraying broadly, since they usually hold scale to tolerable levels on persimmon. Prune out and destroy heavily encrusted wood. A dormant-season horticultural oil application smothers overwintering scale on the bark and is the main direct control for a backyard tree.

beginner: Keep the tree healthy, skip the broad bug sprays that kill the good insects, and check the trunk and branches now and then for the first white crusty patches so you can put on a winter oil spray before it spreads.
seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous, avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that disrupt biological control, and monitor the trunk and scaffolds for early white encrustations so a dormant oil can be timed before populations explode.

beginner: Small soft insects covered in white, cottony fluff, tucked into leaf joints, under the leafy cap of the fruit, and along stems. They leave the same sticky honeydew and black mold as scale, and where they hide under the fruit's cap they can spoil its look.
seasoned: Soft, oval insects coated in white, cottony wax clustered in leaf axils, under the calyx of the fruit, and along shoots. Like scale, they excrete honeydew that fosters sooty mold and ants, and feeding under the calyx can contaminate and blemish fruit.

beginner: Sap-sucking insects called mealybugs that hide in sheltered spots, including under the leafy cap on the fruit. Ants often protect them because they want the sweet honeydew, which lets the mealybugs build up.
seasoned: Mealybugs (several species) that suck phloem sap and shelter in protected crevices, including beneath the fruit calyx. Ant-tended colonies persist because ants protect them from natural enemies for the honeydew.

beginner: Let natural predators handle most mealybugs, and avoid broad sprays that kill those helpers. Stop ants from climbing the trunk with a sticky band so the predators can reach the mealybugs. Dab visible clusters with horticultural oil or insecticidal soap.
seasoned: Rely first on natural enemies, which generally keep mealybugs below damaging levels on landscape fruit trees; avoid the broad-spectrum sprays that disrupt them. Control honeydew-farming ants (sticky trunk bands) so predators can work. Spot-treat visible colonies with a horticultural oil or insecticidal soap.

beginner: Keep the helpful insects around by not spraying broadly, keep ants off the tree, and check under the cap of the growing fruit where mealybugs like to hide, picking off any infested ones early.
seasoned: Maintain biological control by minimizing broad-spectrum sprays, manage ants, and inspect the calyx end of developing fruit where mealybugs hide, removing infested fruit early.

beginner: In spring the new leaves curl and roll up around tiny insects feeding inside. You may see small crawlers and white waxy threads inside the rolled leaves. On an older tree the harm is mostly cosmetic, but it can slow down a young one.
seasoned: New leaves curl, roll, and cup around the feeding of tiny nymphs in spring, often distorting the flush of young growth. Small crawlers and their waxy filaments may be visible inside the rolled leaves. Damage is largely cosmetic on an established tree but can stunt young shoots.

beginner: A small sap-feeding insect called the persimmon psyllid. Its young feed on the new spring leaves and make them curl. It is a minor pest that mostly just looks bad.
seasoned: The persimmon psyllid, a small sap-feeding insect whose nymphs feed on expanding leaves in spring and induce the characteristic leaf roll. It is a minor, mostly cosmetic pest of both native and Oriental persimmon.

beginner: Usually nothing needs to be done, since the tree shrugs it off. On a small tree you can clip off the worst curled tips in spring. Avoid broad sprays so the helpful insects stay around.
seasoned: Usually no treatment is warranted; natural enemies and the tree's vigor absorb the damage. On a small tree, prune off and destroy the worst rolled tips in spring. Preserve beneficial insects by avoiding broad sprays.

beginner: There is not much to do. A healthy tree with its natural predators intact keeps this pest to a harmless nuisance.
seasoned: Little is required. Keeping the tree healthy and preserving natural enemies keeps the psyllid a cosmetic nuisance rather than a problem.

beginner: Shoots that wilt or die, and near the bottom of the trunk a sticky ooze mixed with what looks like sawdust, where the larvae are tunneling under the bark. A young tree can be ringed and killed, so this is the one persimmon pest to take seriously.
seasoned: Wilting or dying shoots and, on the trunk, gummy ooze mixed with sawdust-like frass near the base where larvae tunnel the inner bark. Young trees can be girdled and killed; it is the one persimmon pest extension warns can be serious, particularly in the Southeast.

beginner: The larvae (grub stage) of borer beetles and moths that tunnel into the lower trunk. Wounded or stressed trees are hit hardest, but a healthy tree can be attacked too.
seasoned: Larvae of the persimmon (and flatheaded) borers that bore into the lower trunk and inner bark. Trees stressed by wounds or drought are attacked first, but healthy bark can also be entered; it affects both native and Oriental persimmon.

beginner: Once the larvae are inside, no spray reaches them. Scrape soil away from the base, find the holes marked by gum and sawdust, and kill the grubs with a stiff wire. Keep mowers and trimmers away from the trunk so you are not giving the borers wounds to enter.
seasoned: No spray reaches larvae already inside the trunk. Expose the crown, locate entry holes by the gum and frass, and kill larvae by hand with a wire. Keep the trunk base free of mechanical wounds and remove badly infested young wood.

beginner: Keep mowers and string trimmers off the trunk, keep the tree healthy and watered, and check the base of the trunk each late summer for fresh ooze and sawdust so you catch borers early.
seasoned: Protect the lower trunk from injury, keep the tree vigorous and well watered, and inspect the trunk base each late summer for fresh gum and frass so an infestation is caught in its first year.

beginner: Dark, sunken spots on the fruit and spots or dieback on leaves and new shoots, worst in warm, rainy weather. Bad cases rot the fruit and thin out the leaves.
seasoned: Dark, sunken lesions on fruit, and spots and dieback on leaves and young shoots, most damaging in warm, wet weather and humid regions. Infected fruit can rot before or after harvest, and severe leaf infection thins the canopy.

beginner: A fungus (anthracnose) that survives winter in dead wood and old fruit and spreads in warm, wet weather. It is a bigger problem in humid, rainy areas than in dry ones.
seasoned: Anthracnose fungi (Colletotrichum and related genera) that overwinter in dead wood and mummified fruit and spread by rain-splash in warm, humid conditions. Pressure is highest in the wet Southeast and lowest in dry-summer climates.

beginner: Cleanup is the main fix: cut out dead branches, pick off and throw away any shriveled old fruit, and prune so the tree is open and dries fast after rain. Remove spotted fruit as you see it. A home tree rarely needs spraying if you keep it clean.
seasoned: Sanitation is the core control: prune out and destroy dead and cankered wood and remove mummified fruit, and keep the canopy open so it dries quickly after rain. Remove and dispose of infected fruit promptly. Fungicides are rarely needed on a backyard tree if sanitation is kept up.

beginner: Keep the tree open with light pruning, clean up fallen and dried-up fruit every year, and plant it where air moves freely. In rainy areas, pick a variety known to hold up better.
seasoned: Choose an open canopy through pruning, clear fallen and mummified fruit each season, and site the tree with good air movement. In high-pressure humid regions, favor cultivars with better tolerance.

beginner: A tree that slowly goes downhill, with thin yellow leaves and dying branches, usually in wet or heavy soil. The bark and roots at the base turn dark and rotten. Asian persimmon is especially prone, and a badly affected tree can die within a year or two.
seasoned: General decline, sparse yellowing foliage, and dieback on a tree in heavy or poorly drained soil, with dark, decayed bark and roots at and below the soil line. Asian persimmon is especially susceptible; the tree may collapse over a season or two once the crown is girdled.

beginner: Water-mold fungi in the soil (Phytophthora) that rot the roots and crown when the ground stays wet. Asian persimmon is easily hit, which is why it is often grafted onto the tougher native persimmon roots.
seasoned: Soilborne Phytophthora (and related) fungi that attack roots and the crown in waterlogged soil. Oriental persimmon is notably susceptible to root rot, which is a chief reason it is often grafted onto the more tolerant native (D. virginiana) rootstock.

beginner: Once the base is rotting there is no fixing it, so this one is all about prevention. Never plant where water stands, plant on a raised mound in heavy soil, and pick a tree grafted onto native persimmon roots if your drainage is iffy. Do not overwater an older tree.
seasoned: There is no cure once the crown is rotting. Management is prevention through drainage: never plant in standing-water sites, plant on a mound in heavy soil, and choose a tree on tolerant native rootstock where drainage is marginal. Avoid overwatering an established tree.

beginner: Plant only where water drains well, or on a raised mound, choose a tree on native persimmon rootstock if your soil is heavy, and water deeply now and then instead of keeping the soil soggy.
seasoned: Plant only on well-drained ground or a raised berm, select tolerant (native) rootstock in marginal soils, and water deeply but infrequently rather than keeping the root zone saturated.

beginner: Round or angular spots on the leaves that can turn them yellow and drop in a wet year, plus a little dieback of small twigs. On a healthy persimmon this is usually minor and just cosmetic.
seasoned: Circular to angular leaf spots that may yellow and drop leaves in a wet season, and dieback of small twigs. Usually a minor, cosmetic issue on an otherwise healthy persimmon, which extension sources note has few serious disease problems.

beginner: Common leaf-spot fungi that show up when leaves stay wet a long time. Persimmon has few real disease problems, so this is usually just a minor, weather-related annoyance.
seasoned: Several leaf-spot fungi favored by prolonged leaf wetness. Persimmon is generally regarded as having no serious insect or disease problems, so leaf spot is typically a low-impact, weather-driven nuisance.

beginner: Rake up and remove fallen spotted leaves, keep the tree open, and keep it healthy. A home tree almost never needs a spray for this.
seasoned: Rake and remove fallen infected leaves to reduce carryover, keep the canopy open, and keep the tree vigorous; fungicides are seldom justified on a home tree.

beginner: Good airflow, light pruning to keep the tree open, and cleaning up fallen leaves in autumn keep this to a harmless level.
seasoned: Good air movement, an open canopy, and fall leaf cleanup keep leaf spot to a cosmetic level.

beginner: Water deeply now and then rather than a little every day. A young tree needs a deep soak about once or twice a week for its first couple of years. An older tree handles dry spells well and is happy with roughly a weekly deep soak in summer, less when it is cool, and almost nothing in winter. Do not keep the soil soggy, since that causes root rot.
seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently. A young tree wants a deep soak about once or twice a week through its first two seasons; an established tree is fairly drought-tolerant and does well on roughly weekly deep watering in summer heat, less in cool weather and little through winter dormancy. Persimmon prefers infrequent, thorough irrigation over frequent shallow watering, and standing-wet soil invites root rot.

beginner: Each time you water, give a deep soak that reaches down to the roots, not just a splash on top. A young tree wants about 5 gallons per soak; an older, fruiting tree wants about an inch of water a week through the growing season, and more in a heat wave. Deep soaks build deep roots that handle dry spells.
seasoned: Soak deeply enough to wet the full root zone rather than just the surface: on the order of 5 gallons per watering for a young tree, and roughly the equivalent of an inch of water per week for a bearing tree through the growing season, more in extreme heat. Deep, thorough soaks drive the deep rooting that carries an established persimmon through dry stretches.

beginner: Water the ground around the roots with a drip line or soaker hose, out to the edge of the branches, and keep the base of the trunk from sitting wet. Persimmon handles dry better than soggy, so let the soil dry a bit between waterings. In humid areas, avoid spraying water over the leaves, which can bring on leaf diseases.
seasoned: Water at the root zone with drip or a soaker hose out toward the drip line, keeping the trunk base from staying wet. Persimmon tolerates drought better than waterlogging, so the discipline is deep-then-dry, never continuously saturated. Overhead watering that wets the canopy in humid regions can encourage anthracnose and leaf spot.

beginner: Yellow leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and a tree slowly going downhill mean too much water and the risk of root rot, which persimmon catches easily. Soil that never dries out is your signal to back off. Overwatering hurts persimmon more than underwatering does.
seasoned: Yellowing leaves, wilting that persists in wet soil, and general decline point to waterlogging and possible root or crown rot, to which persimmon (especially Asian types) is prone. Soil that never dries between waterings is the warning; this is far more dangerous to persimmon than underwatering.

beginner: Wilting, dull or curling leaves, slower growth, and, the clearest sign, fruit dropping early or staying small when the tree gets too dry while the fruit is filling out. An older persimmon can take some dryness, but the crop suffers if it goes too dry for too long.
seasoned: Wilting, dull or curling leaves, slowed growth, and, most tellingly, premature fruit drop or small, poorly sized fruit when a tree runs dry during fruit development. An established persimmon endures moderate drought but sizes its crop poorly under sustained water stress.

beginner: While the tree is getting established, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps it grow the deep roots it needs.
seasoned: Through establishment, keep the root ball and surrounding soil evenly moist but never waterlogged. Deep soaks of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, adjusted for rain and heat, build the deep root system persimmon relies on later.

beginner: While the fruit is sizing up, keep the water steady. Letting the tree swing from dry to wet now can make the fruit drop or stay small. Aim for about an inch of water a week as deep soaks, more when it is hot.
seasoned: During fruit development, keep moisture steady; sudden drought or a wet-dry swing in this window contributes to premature fruit drop and small fruit. Aim for the equivalent of about an inch of water a week, delivered as deep soaks, more in heat.

beginner: After the leaves fall and the tree is resting, it needs very little water. Let rain do most of the work and only water in long dry stretches. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.
seasoned: Once the tree drops its leaves and goes dormant, water need falls sharply; rely mostly on rainfall and water only in prolonged dry spells. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated, which favors root rot.

beginner: Give deep soaks now and then rather than a little every day, and water at the ground with a drip line or soaker hose, letting the soil dry out a bit between waterings. Persimmon handles dry much better than soggy. Young trees need steady moisture for their first couple of years; older trees take dry spells but drop fruit if left too dry too long.
seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently at the root zone, ideally by drip or soaker, to encourage deep rooting; let the soil dry between waterings, since persimmon tolerates drought far better than waterlogging. Young trees need consistent moisture through their first two seasons; established trees are moderately drought-tolerant but drop fruit and size poorly under sustained stress.

beginner: Firm-eaten types like Fuyu keep on the counter for a week or more and just slowly soften. Astringent types like Hachiya need to sit out until they turn completely soft and jelly-like before you eat them, or they taste harshly puckery. Persimmons keep ripening after picking, so leaving astringent ones on the counter to soften is exactly right.
seasoned: Non-astringent types (Fuyu) are eaten firm and hold at room temperature for a week or more, softening slowly. Astringent types (Hachiya) must be held at room temperature until they ripen to a jelly-soft, fully translucent stage before eating; rushing them leaves an intensely puckery, tannic mouthfeel. Persimmons continue to ripen after picking, so counter-ripening astringent fruit is normal practice.

beginner: Firm Fuyu-type persimmons keep in the fridge for several weeks, better than most fruit. Put soft, ripe Hachiya-type fruit in the fridge only once it is fully soft, and eat it within a few days.
seasoned: Refrigerate firm non-astringent persimmons to hold them for several weeks; they keep notably better than most tree fruit. Refrigerate soft-ripe astringent fruit only once fully ripe and use within a few days. Chilling can be used to speed some astringent types toward ripeness, but eating quality is best judged by full softness.

beginner: Persimmons freeze nicely as pulp. Scoop out the soft ripe flesh, mix in a little lemon juice so it does not brown, and freeze it in portions. It keeps for months and is great for baking. You can also freeze whole astringent persimmons; thawing softens them and takes away the pucker.
seasoned: Persimmons freeze well as pulp. Scoop the soft, ripe flesh of astringent types, or puree non-astringent flesh, add a little lemon juice to limit browning, and freeze in portions. Frozen pulp keeps for several months and is ideal for baking, cookies, and puddings. Whole astringent fruit can also be frozen and thawed, which softens and de-astringes them.

beginner: The number one persimmon mistake is eating an astringent kind before it is completely soft, which is harshly puckery. Eat firm types like Fuyu crisp, and let soft types like Hachiya ripen all the way first.
seasoned: The single most common persimmon disappointment is biting an astringent Hachiya-type before it is fully soft. Match handling to type: eat non-astringent Fuyu firm, ripen astringent types to jelly-soft first.

beginner: Pick first by type and your climate. In zone 7 and warmer, an Asian persimmon is usually best: a self-fruitful, non-astringent Fuyu to eat crisp, or an astringent Hachiya to eat soft. In colder areas (zones 4 to 6), choose an American persimmon: a self-fruitful Meader for a single tree, or a hardy kind like Prok with a male tree nearby. Persimmon needs little winter cold, so most types suit most winters. Buy a named, grafted tree rather than a seedling so you know the fruit and, for American types, the sex.
seasoned: Choose first by type and climate. In zones 7 and warmer, an Asian persimmon (D. kaki) is the usual pick: a self-fruitful, non-astringent Fuyu for firm crisp eating, or an astringent Hachiya for soft-ripe fruit and baking. In colder zones (4 to 6), choose an American persimmon (D. virginiana): a self-fruitful Meader for a single tree, or a hardy female such as Prok with a male pollinizer. Match the cultivar's modest chill requirement to your winters, and favor named grafted cultivars over seedlings for known fruit quality and sex.

beginner: Hardening off (slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to being outside) does not apply to persimmon. You plant it as a dormant bare-root tree or a young grafted tree from a pot, not as a seedling started inside, so there is no tender plant to ease outdoors.
seasoned: Hardening off does not apply to persimmon. It is planted as a dormant bare-root or grafted container tree, not raised from a seedling indoors, so there is no tender transplant to acclimate to the outdoors.

beginner: Plant a bare-root tree in late winter or early spring while it is still leafless, or set a young potted grafted tree in the cooler months. Persimmon does not like having its roots disturbed, so handle them gently and plant it right away. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them, set the tree at the same depth it grew before with the graft joint above the soil, fill in with the soil you dug out, and water it in well. Do not put fertilizer in the hole. If your soil is heavy, plant on a raised mound so water drains away.
seasoned: Plant a dormant bare-root tree in late winter to early spring before bud break, or set a grafted container tree in the cooler months. Persimmon resents root disturbance, so handle the taproot gently and plant promptly. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them, set the tree at the depth it grew in the nursery with the graft union above the final soil line, backfill with native soil, water in well, and do not fertilize in the planting hole. On heavy soil, plant on a raised mound for drainage.

beginner: If you grow a dwarf persimmon in a pot, use a chunky, fast-draining mix made for shrubs and trees, not a soft peat-based potting soil that stays soggy. A bark-based mix (composted bark with perlite or pumice for drainage) gives the roots the air they need. Do not use soil dug from the yard in a pot, because it packs down and drains poorly.
seasoned: For a container persimmon (a genetic-dwarf or size-controlled tree), use a coarse, fast-draining soilless mix built for woody plants, not a peat-heavy potting soil. A bark-based mix (composted pine bark with perlite or pumice) supplies the air-filled porosity persimmon roots need; the species is root-rot-prone, so the mix must never stay saturated. Skip native garden soil, which compacts under container irrigation.

seasoned: Keep amendments minimal and drainage-first: add perlite or pumice if the base mix is water-retentive, and top-dress with a thin layer of compost rather than blending heavy organics throughout. Avoid moisture-retentive crystals or large peat fractions, which work against the free-draining root zone persimmon demands.

beginner: A persimmon in a pot dries out much faster than one in the ground. In summer heat, check it daily and water when the top inch or two is dry, until water runs out the bottom, but never let the pot stand in a saucer of water, since wet roots rot. In winter, when the tree is resting, give just enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
seasoned: A potted persimmon dries far faster than one in the ground and has no deep soil to draw on, so check moisture daily in summer heat and water when the top inch or two is dry, until it runs from the drainage holes. Water more often than an in-ground tree, but never leave the pot standing in a full saucer, because continuously wet roots rot. Through dormancy the tree needs only enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.

seasoned: Frequent watering flushes nutrients from a pot, so feed lightly and stop by late summer to avoid pushing tender growth into fall. Persimmon is a light feeder and excess nitrogen drops fruit, so keep container feeding conservative: a dilute balanced liquid feed a few times through the spring-to-midsummer flush is ample.

It can be done, but expect more hands-on watering and smaller crops. Use the biggest well-draining pot you can, and give it winter protection in cold areas.
